reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A slow-growing photochromogen originally isolated from monkeys, hence its name
Its main reservoir is water, including aquifers and tap water, and it shows geographical clustering in certain regions
Very commonly isolated as an environmental contaminant or coloniser, so true disease is far less frequent than positive cultures suggest
When genuinely pathogenic it causes nodular-bronchiectatic or cavitary pulmonary disease and, in the profoundly immunosuppressed, disseminated infection
Notoriously drug-resistant, with unpredictable in vitro susceptibility and a poor response to treatment
Distinguishing colonisation from disease is a central challenge and requires strict application of diagnostic criteria
When treatment is warranted, susceptibility-guided combinations (often including a macrolide, moxifloxacin, and co-trimoxazole) are used, but results are frequently disappointing
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium simiae is a slow-growing photochromogenic mycobacterium whose reservoir is water, including groundwater aquifers and municipal supplies, giving rise to regional clusters. It is among the mycobacteria most often recovered as a contaminant or airway coloniser, and only a minority of positive cultures reflect true disease. When pathogenic it produces chronic pulmonary infection in hosts with structural lung disease and disseminated disease in the profoundly immunosuppressed. Intrinsic and unpredictable drug resistance, with poor correlation between in vitro testing and clinical response, makes it one of the more difficult nontuberculous mycobacteria to treat.
additionalDifferentials: Colonisation or contamination without true disease
additionalInvestigations: Repeated respiratory cultures to distinguish colonisation from genuine disease
Mycobacterial culture with recognition of photochromogenic pigment
Drug-susceptibility testing, recognising its limited predictive value
Chest CT for nodular-bronchiectatic or cavitary disease
Assessment of immune status, particularly for disseminated disease
redFlags: Progressive pulmonary disease meeting diagnostic criteria
Poor response to therapy reflecting extensive drug resistance
Clustered isolates suggesting a shared water source
reference.prognosis: Even when true disease is confirmed, response to treatment is often poor because of extensive and unpredictable drug resistance, so the prognosis is guarded. Many isolates, however, represent colonisation that does not require treatment and does not progress.
pitfalls: Treating a coloniser or contaminant as genuine disease and exposing the patient to prolonged toxic therapy
Relying too heavily on in vitro susceptibility that correlates poorly with outcome
Failing to meet diagnostic criteria before starting treatment
Underestimating the difficulty of achieving cure
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Distinguish colonisation or contamination from genuine disease by strict diagnostic criteria and repeated respiratory cultures, since many isolates need no treatment

When true disease is confirmed, use multidrug therapy such as a macrolide with a fluoroquinolone like moxifloxacin and co-trimoxazole, recognising the poor correlation between in vitro susceptibility and response
Aim for disease control rather than reliable cure given the notorious and unpredictable drug resistance
Manage the underlying structural lung disease alongside antimycobacterial treatment
Monitor treatment response with repeated cultures and watch for drug toxicity over the prolonged course
Assess immune status, particularly where disseminated disease is suspected in profoundly immunosuppressed patients
Refer to infectious diseases or respiratory medicine given the guarded prognosis and treatment difficulty
